tests.name: Sun and Earth positions vs NASA JPL Horizons
tests.what: Azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth from 6 sites, every 7h from 2026-01-01 00:00 to 2026-06-01 00:00 UTC (6216 comparisons). Ours: SPICE (DE440, MOON_ME, CN+S) + pipeline/geometry.py. Horizons: coord@301, QUANTITIES 4, airless.
tests.explanation: Largest angle on the sky between our direction and Horizons'. Small remaining differences come from light-time measured from the Moon's centre (ours) vs from the site (Horizons) and from Horizons' gravitational light bending.

tests.name: Browser engine vs Python/SPICE (1,000 cases)
tests.what: 1,000 random and edge-case sites, heights and times (many between hours), computed with SPICE in Python (pipeline/golden.py) and recomputed by the TypeScript engine.
tests.tolerance: every case within 0.001 deg (Sun and Earth azimuth, elevation, separation)
tests.explanation: 1000 cases, worst gap 0.000125 deg (limit 0.001). The small gap comes from blending hourly direction vectors between hours and from storing positions as 32-bit numbers. The browser's fixed TDB offset differs from SPICE by at most 1.66 ms (the TDB-TT periodic term), about 0.0000002 deg of Sun motion.

tests.name: Time trap: UTC fed in as TDB
tests.what: V1 for the equator Sun again, but every time is shifted by -69.184 s, the mistake of treating clock time (UTC) as TDB.
tests.tolerance: must exceed the V1 target of 0.002 deg (expected about 0.0098 deg)
tests.explanation: The Sun crosses the lunar sky at about 0.0085 deg per minute, so a 69.2 s clock mistake moves it about 0.0098 deg. This test failing proves V1 is sensitive enough to catch time-scale bugs.

tests.name: Sun height at the exact pole (smooth Moon)
tests.what: Sun height every 6 h, 2023-2032, a hair from 90 S, no terrain, no mast.
tests.explanation: At the pole the Sun never rises more than the tilt of the Moon's equator allows. The plan expected 1.54 deg (the mean tilt, 1.543 deg); the true maximum is larger because of physical libration and the Moon's orbital tilt. The day-one kernel check found 1.587 deg in both MOON_ME and IAU_MOON (docs/kernel_checks.txt), so the expected value was corrected to 1.59 deg. Against the original 1.54 deg this test would fail.

tests.name: Equator (0, 0), smooth Moon
tests.what: Every 10 minutes, 2023-2032, 2 m mast, any part of the Sun counts as up.
tests.tolerance: Sun up 50 +/- 0.5 %; mean day 14.77 +/- 0.4 d; Earth always up, at least ~79 deg high
tests.explanation: Mean day 14.85 d over 122 complete lunar days (slightly over 14.77 d because the Sun's edge and the mast add minutes at each end). Earth stays at least 79.56 deg high. Eclipses (72.8 h in the decade) darken the Sun but are not counted as sunsets.

tests.name: Far side (Chang'e-4): Earth never visible
tests.what: Earth's height every hour, 2023-2032, at 45.4446 S, 177.5991 E (Liu et al. 2019), smooth Moon.
tests.tolerance: no part of Earth ever above the horizon; centre about -37 to -53 deg
tests.explanation: Earth's centre stays between -51.6 and -37.1 deg (mean -44.5 deg): libration rocks it up and down but never brings it close to the horizon. Direct-to-Earth contact is impossible there, which is why Chang'e-4 needed the Queqiao relay satellite.

tests.name: Total lunar eclipse of 2025-03-14 seen from the Moon
tests.what: Fraction of the Sun not covered by Earth, every minute 06:26-07:31 UTC, at (0, 0).
tests.explanation: During totality the whole Moon is in Earth's shadow, so Earth hides the Sun completely. At this single point the Sun is covered from 2025-03-14T05:45:00 to 2025-03-14T08:10:00 UTC, longer than totality, which needs the whole Moon inside the shadow. Earth is drawn as a solid disc (no atmosphere).

tests.name: Apollo 11 landing: Sun and Earth in the sky
tests.what: Sun and Earth seen from Tranquility Base (0.67408 N, 23.47297 E) at touchdown, 1969-07-20 20:17:40 UTC. Python only: the app's ephemeris starts in 2023.
tests.tolerance: Sun about 10.8-11 deg high, within 1 deg; azimuth about 88 deg; Earth about 60-66 deg
tests.explanation: Sun 10.70 deg high at azimuth 88.8 deg, low in the east, as NASA planned so that long shadows showed the terrain. Earth 59.2 deg high, just under the plan's 'about 60-66 deg' estimate.

tests.name: Connecting Ridge average sunlight vs published research
tests.what: Average visible part of the Sun's disc, every hour 2023-2032, at 89.4395 S, 222.8066 E, 2 m mast, using M3's LOLA horizon mask.
tests.tolerance: within 5 points of about 88% (Glaser et al. 2018)
tests.explanation: Ours 87.9% vs about 88% published. Longest continuous darkness 4.71 d vs 4.58 d in Glaser et al. 2014, who used a different period. Differences come from the terrain model and the years averaged.

tests.name: Mission replay: IM-1 Odysseus
tests.what: IM-1 at 80.13 S, 1.44 E with M3's LOLA mask, 22 Feb - 6 Mar 2024. Plausibility check: the lander's end of operations (about 29 Feb) should come no later than the computed loss of the Sun.
tests.tolerance: Sun visible at landing; operations ended on or before the computed Sun loss
tests.unit: h between end of operations and computed Sun loss
tests.explanation: Terrain hides the Sun from 2024-03-02T18:00:00Z, about 66 h after operations ended. IM-1 tipped over, so its panels lost the Sun before the terrain did. Not a sunset: the lander stopped for a different reason.

tests.name: Mission replay: Chandrayaan-3 Vikram
tests.what: Vikram at the ISRO and the LROC coordinates (about 360 m apart), 23 Aug - 26 Sep 2023. Plausibility check: the computed sunset should come after it was put to sleep on 4 Sep, and the computed sunrise should fall near ISRO's expected 22 Sep.
tests.tolerance: Sun visible at landing; sunset after the 4 Sep sleep; sunrise within 3 days of 22 Sep
tests.explanation: The Sun reaches the horizon about 1.8 days before ISRO's date (0.85 deg high on 20 Sep, 9.11 deg on 22 Sep), so 22 Sep matches when it is usefully high. The plan allowed 1 day; we use 3 days because sunrise at this latitude is slow and ISRO's date is a rounded forecast, and we say so rather than hide the 1.8-day gap. The two coordinate sets differ by only a few hours.

tests.name: Mission replay: IM-2 Athena and the 14 March 2025 eclipse
tests.what: IM-2 at 84.7906 S, 29.1957 E with M3's LOLA mask, 6 - 21 Mar 2025. Plausibility check: the 14 Mar total lunar eclipse should show as a dip to near zero sunlight.
tests.tolerance: Sun visible at landing; Sun covered by Earth (below 5% visible) on 14 Mar
tests.explanation: Earth covers the Sun from about 05:40 to 08:20 UTC on 14 Mar. This is geometry only: IM-2 ended within about 13 h of landing, so the eclipse did not cause its end. Eclipses are drawn as their own dip, not as a sunset.

tests.name: DSN: Moon height at Goldstone vs JPL Horizons
tests.what: Elevation of the Moon above the horizon at DSS-14 (Goldstone) every hour on 2026-11-14, read from the shipped dsn.bin and compared with JPL Horizons (observer on Earth, airless, quantity 4).
tests.explanation: Worst gap 0.0048 deg over 25 hours. Station coordinates for Horizons come from the NAIF station kernel itself, so a gap would mean a frame or time mistake. DSN contact needs the Moon above 6, 10.1 or 13.6 deg, so 0.05 deg is far inside what matters.
